title: The Borrowed Undertow
premise: Dominic Dunmore, a translator raised in a coastal village where his grandmother spoke a fading creole, has spent thirty years cataloguing words he never said to her before she died. When the house she raised him in — and the creole-speaking foster siblings she took in — goes up for auction and demolition, Dominic returns to buy it back, only to discover his estranged foster sister Nkechi holds the deed and a grievance he cannot translate. As the auction deadline collides with the anniversary of the fire that killed their foster brother, Dominic must finally render the unsayable sentence — his confession of what he saw that night — and choose between the family he abandoned and the duty that made him leave. He loses the house but gains back the language, speaking his confession aloud at the demolition, where Nkechi, hearing him in their grandmother's creole for the first time, finally lets him come home.
about_author: Ada Okonkwo is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between Lagos and a fading coastal town, writing about the words families lose in transit. Their work has appeared in several literary journals, and this is their first novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Dominic, in his London flat, works on a legal translation while maintaining his private ledger of unspoken words to his late grandmother. A solicitor's letter arrives: the house on Meridian Row enters auction in six weeks, demolition scheduled after. POV: Dominic. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional calm — the past has issued a deadline.

chapters.title: Meridian Row
chapters.summary: Dominic returns to the coastal town after thirty years, walking the salt-crusted streets and finding the house boarded but standing. He encounters old neighbor Mrs. Adeyemi, who reveals Nkechi never left the town — and never forgave him. POV: Dominic. Emotional beat: the vertigo of return; home is both smaller and heavier than memory.

chapters.title: The Deed in Her Name
chapters.summary: Dominic confronts Nkechi at her boatyard, learning she co-inherited the house and refuses to sell to him. Flashback threads: the four foster children, grandmother's creole, the night of the fire that killed Sami. POV: alternating Dominic and Nkechi. Emotional beat: two griefs, one house, neither willing to translate for the other.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Dominic lodges above the town's failing bakery, run by Teo, a warm widower who feeds him and asks nothing. Dominic begins losing creole words from memory — the ledger now records words he can no longer recall at all. POV: Dominic. Emotional beat: found family flickering to life in Teo's kitchen, against the guilt of the family he left.

chapters.title: What the Fire Kept
chapters.summary: Nkechi's POV chapter: the fire's full story from her side — how Sami died, how Dominic vanished the next morning, how she raised herself on silence. She has kept Sami's belongings in the house, the real reason she won't let it fall. POV: Nkechi. Emotional beat: her love for Dominic curdled into duty to the dead.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Dominic bids against a developer, spending everything, and loses by a single increment to a shell company — which he discovers belongs to Nkechi, who bought the house to control its destruction on her own terms. POV: Dominic. Emotional beat: public humiliation that cracks his composure; the first time he raises his voice in years.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Drunk on Teo's porch, Dominic admits the truth he has never written in the ledger: he saw Sami enter the house that night and said nothing, afraid of his own implication. Teo tells him a sentence unspoken in one language can still be spoken in another. POV: Dominic. Emotional beat: the confession surfaces — but only in English, the coward's tongue.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: Nkechi, alone in the house with Sami's things, finds Dominic's childhood ledger hidden in the floorboards — decades of unsaid words, ending mid-sentence. She reads it through the night. POV: Nkechi. Emotional beat: fury dissolving into recognition; his silence was a prison, not an escape.

chapters.title: The Wrecking Ball
chapters.summary: At the demolition, before the crowd and the machines, Dominic steps forward and delivers the untranslatable sentence in their grandmother's creole — the confession, and the apology, and Sami's name. The house comes down as he speaks. POV: Dominic. Emotional beat: climax — the language returns exactly when he needs it, and costs him everything to use.

chapters.title: What We Keep by Giving Away
chapters.summary: Weeks later: Nkechi and Dominic sort Sami's salvaged things in Teo's bakery, planning a memorial garden on the empty lot. Dominic begins a new ledger — this one of things said. POV: Dominic, with a final Nkechi passage. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; justice outside the law, love chosen over duty, family rebuilt on spoken words.
